title: Shadow rollout tokenizer normalization regression writeup
content:
Summary:

This writeup documents an incident discovered during a shadow rollout in late August: a subtle token normalization change in a new tokenizer variant caused embeddings drift (recall drop) for a subset of customer queries. The change did not raise our standard canary health checks because latency and error-rate SLOs remained within bounds; the regression manifested as reduced semantic retrieval recall and a rise in interestingly coherent but incorrect reranks.

Impact:
- Effected surface: embedding similarity and downstream reranker quality on the embeddings-v2 model family when the new tokenizer was used as a preprocessor.
- Customer-visible: 2 customers reported degraded retrievals for Korean/multi-byte whitespace queries; internal synthetic recall tests showed a ~9-12% drop on a seed query set.
- Availability/latency: no CPU/GPU resource regressions, p95/p99 latency unchanged.

How it was detected:
- Customer Slack -> Support escalation reporting confusing retrievals for non-English inputs.
- An on-call engineer (Asha) triaged and ran a small offline embedding-sim test and reproduced a recall drop with the canary tokenizer enabled in shadow.
- The shadow metrics pipeline flagged a divergence in token sequence length distribution for the same input between baseline and canary tokenizers.

Timeline (abridged):
- 2024-08-28 09:12: Shadow rollout triggered for tokenizer v1.12 (config: normalize_spaces=True, canonicalize_nfc=True).
- 2024-08-28 12:34 First customer report (support).
- 2024-08-28 13:05 On-call begins triage; reproduces recall drop locally using sample set.
- 2024-08-28 14:40 Confirmed token sequence mismatch concentrated on multi-byte whitespace and combined diacritics.
- 2024-08-28 16:20 Hotfix plan: deploy normalization shim at inference gateway to emulate baseline behavior for affected routes.
- 2024-08-28 18:00 Shim rolled to 20% traffic in gateway (shadow + shadow verification).
- 2024-08-28 20:15 Observed recovery in synthetic recall for those queries.
- 2024-08-29 10:00 Full rollback of tokenizer variant from canary fleet; follow-up PR with rework of normalization landed.

Analysis & Root Cause:
- The tokenizer change introduced a normalization step that collapsed some multi-byte whitespace sequences and applied NFC normalization earlier in the pipeline. Baseline tokenizer applied normalization downstream during model tokenization which caused small differences in byte-level token ids for certain scripts (notably Korean + combining diacritics).
- Effects: different token boundaries led to different token ids, leading the embedding model to produce different vectors and therefore downstream similarity distances shifted enough to fail threshold-based retrieval heuristics.
- Why canary health checks missed it: our standard canary suite focuses on latency, memory, error rates, and tokenization checksum equality for ASCII/English seed. We did not run a targeted embedding-similarity regression test or non-English token-distribution checks as part of the canary.
- Additional compounding factor: the tokenizer config fingerprinting used to gate rollout was based on timestamped artifact names; a minor packaging step changed the tokenizer binary build timestamp, so the rollout gating UI showed the expected fingerprint even though the runtime behavior changed (packaging discrepancy).

Immediate Mitigation & Rollback:
1) Gateway normalization shim (short-term): implemented a lightweight pre-tokenizer shim that applied the baseline normalization rules to inputs for affected routes. This shim lived in the inference gateway (stateless) and could be toggled via feature-flag. Deployed to 20% traffic shadow and verified equality of token sequences with baseline.
2) Full rollback: removed tokenizer v1.12 from canary fleet and halted rollout across clusters.
3) Customer communication: support notified impacted customers with initial workaround and ETA for full fix.

Why the shim was chosen:
- Fast to deploy (no model reload), reversible, and allowed us to continue collecting shadow comparison telemetry while preventing further customer exposure.

Post-incident actions (short to mid term):
- Add embedding-sanity tests to canary suite: for every tokenizer/model pair added to canary, run a small set (~200) of multilingual seed queries (including Korean, combining diacritics, and CJK punctuation) and compare cosine similarity distributions to baseline; fail rollout if mean similarity drops > 5% or if >15% of queries drop below a per-query threshold.
- Tokenizer fingerprinting hardening: replace timestamp/name-based fingerprint with a deterministic content hash (sha256) of the tokenizer config + binary blobs used at runtime. Include that hash in rollout manifests and require exact match to proceed.
- Expand shadow telemetry: record token sequence histograms by language/Unicode-range and compare baseline vs canary deltas automatically. Add alerting for unexpected shifts.
- Add a new 'normalization-compatibility' smoke-check to serving-runtime CI that runs both normalization-first and normalization-later flows and ensures token id parity for a representative unicode corpus.
- Update documentation: describe normalization ordering guarantees (what the runtime guarantees about NFC/NFD and whitespace collapsing) so model teams and tokenizer authors have clear constraints.

Runbook changes (items to add):
- "If embedding recall drops without latency or error spikes, run token-sequence parity check between baseline and canary": include exact curl commands and scripts (see quick commands below).
- Add a step to check tokenizer artifact content-hash match between baseline and canary before allowing traffic ramp.
- When using shadow rollouts for tokenizer or tokenization-sensitive changes, enable multilingual sample set checks in the shadow pipeline by default.

On-call notes & quick reproducible commands (for responders):
- Reproduce token sequence diff (example):
  curl -s -X POST https://inference-gateway.internal/v1/tokenize -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"embeddings-v2","input":"한국어  테스트 with́combine"}' | jq '.' > /tmp/canary_tokens.json
  curl -s -X POST https://inference-gateway-internal/v1/tokenize?variant=baseline -H "Content-Type: application/json" -d '{"model":"embeddings-v2","input":"한국어  테스트 with́combine"}' | jq '.' > /tmp/baseline_tokens.json
  diff /tmp/baseline_tokens.json /tmp/canary_tokens.json || true
- Quick embedding similarity check (local):
  python tools/sim_check.py --baseline /tmp/baseline_vectors.npy --candidate /tmp/canary_vectors.npy --min-mean-sim 0.88
- Toggle gateway shim (feature-flag):
  curl -X POST https://ops-api.internal/feature-flag -H "Authorization: Bearer $TOKEN" -d '{"flag":"gateway-token-normalization-shim","state":"on","percentage":20}'

Lessons learned / Notes:
- Shadow rollouts are invaluable; they surfaced a subtle semantic regression that would have been invisible to traditional resource/error canaries. We need to expand what we consider a 'healthy rollout' beyond resource metrics.
- Tokenization changes can have large downstream effects even when they look innocuous at the byte-level; multiple independent checks (checksum, content-hash, semantic tests) are necessary.
- Packaging differences can mask behavioral diffs; deterministic artifact hashes remove a broad class of rollout surprises.

Follow-ups (owners & ETA):
- eng-serving-runtime: implement deterministic tokenizer content-hash gating in rollout manifests (owner: Marcus Chen) — ETA 2024-09-18
- eng-applied-ml: author multilingual embedding-sanity testset and add to canary suite (owner: Priya Singh) — ETA 2024-09-25
- eng-sre: add token-sequence histogram telemetry and related alerting (owner: Elena Rivera) — ETA 2024-10-02
- docs: publish normalization ordering guide and a checklist for tokenizer authors (owner: Liam O'Connor) — ETA 2024-09-30

Appendix: Observed sample diffs (redacted)
- Input: "한국어  테스트 with́combine"
- Baseline tokens: ["▁한국", "어", "▁테스트", " ", "▁with", "́combine"]
- Canary tokens: ["▁한국", "어", "▁테스트 with", "́combine"]
- Note: token boundary shift caused embedding delta large enough to fall below retrieval cutoff for seeded queries.

If you are triaging this in the future: prioritize reproducing token boundaries first (fast) before assuming model weight or kv-cache corruption (slower, higher-impact).
